newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bank of Thailand sees 1997 economic recovery.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Thailand sees 1997 economic recovery.

text.p: Thailand's central bank said on Thursday it saw a moderate recovery for the national economy in 1997 after projecting the slowest growth in a decade for this year and vowing an austerity drive.
Bank of Thailand governor Rerngchai Marakanond said he expected the Thai gross domestic product (GDP) to expand 7.1 percent in 1997, up from about 6.7 percent in 1996.
Exports will grow 7.7 percent next year, helped by more active world trade, after a 0.1 percent contraction in 1996.
"We must admit the economy slowed down in 1996 but it was an adjustment to achieve stability and to prepare for recovery next year," he told a news conference.

"I expect to see early signs of recovery from the second quarter of 1997 and it will become more evident in the third quarter," he said, adding he expected interest rates to come down as well next year.
The recovery would result from a substantial increase in liquidity in the financial market next March as more public sector pension funds invested money locally, he said.
Rerngchai said one of his austerity plans was a proposal for the government to shelve what he called low-priority projects requiring big foreign exchange spending next year.

If Thailand delayed spending 28 billion baht ($1.1 billion) on new commercial aircraft and another 12 billion baht on military expenditure planned for 1997, its current account deficit could narrow to 7.5 percent of GDP from the 7.9 percent projected by the central bank for next year, he said.
The governor said he agreed with Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan's policy to rely mainly on fiscal, rather than monetary measures, to maintain economic and currency stability.

Rerngchai was responding to private sector complaints that a central bank policy of encouraging high Thai interest rates in early 1996 had hurt small business, aggravated problems in the ailing property sector and worsened an economic slowdown.

The governor said despite a dismal export performance in 1996, the government had managed, through monetary discipline, to keep the current account deficit under control and slow a rise in Thai foreign debt.
Total foreign debt rose about $6.0 billion in the first 11 months of 1996 to $88.6 billion at end-November against a $17 billion increase in the previous 12 months to $81.8 billion.
The governor said the current account deficit had shown a declining trend in the second half of 1996, to 30.2 billion baht in October from a monthly peak of 49.6 billion in April.

Analysts described Rerngchai's projections as optimistic. Although sharing his forecast of an economic recovery from the second quarter of 1997, they said the expected slightly higher GDP growth would leave little room for trimming the current account deficit.

"They are a touch optimistic. Things will get worse before getting better...he said interest rates would come down because of (investment by) state provident funds. But I think interest rates would ease because of slow credit demand," said James Marshal, head of research at Capital Nomura Securities.
